source: Lin et al. (2025) MetaLadder: Ascending Mathematical Solution Quality via Analogical-Problem Reasoning Transfer (Findings of EMNLP 2025)
finding: The problem-restating step is the largest single ablation in MetaLadder, but every reported result is from fine-tuned models. The analogous problem is generated by GPT-4o-mini, not retrieved from a memory. The paper has no prompting-only baseline, so it cannot say whether restating works without training.
numbers: LLaMA3-8B fine-tuned, Table 2: full 66.2 GSM8K / 22.4 MATH / 44.3 average; without restate 61.6 / 22.0 / 41.8 (-2.5 average, largest of three ablations). Table 1 averages over six sets: LLaMA3-8B CoT 36.1 vs MetaLadder 39.4 vs best variant 42.5; DeepSeekMath-7B CoT 47.3 vs 52.1 vs 57.6. Analogue generation: GPT-4o-mini, temperature 0.7.
limits: Read through a page extraction of the arXiv HTML, tables not re-checked in the PDF. Fine-tuned only. Restate gain is on GSM8K (+4.6), almost zero on MATH (+0.4). Does not isolate 'abstract the probe before search'.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 stays open for training-free use. The restate step is cheap to copy (one extra generated paragraph) but nothing here shows it helps a frozen model.

source: Su et al. (2025, ICLR) BRIGHT: A Realistic and Challenging Benchmark for Reasoning-Intensive Retrieval
finding: Training-free query rewriting helps a lot when relevance depends on a hidden principle. Asking an LLM to state the essential problem, reason about what a relevant document would contain and draft an answer, then searching with that text, raises nDCG@10 for several retrievers. BM25 gains most, which the authors tie to BM25 adapting to any query while trained embedders see the long LLM text as out of distribution.
numbers: Abstract: reasoning-step queries improve retrieval by up to 12.2 points. BM25 average 14.5 with the original query; the best score on the board with GPT-4 reasoning as query is still below 30. Llama-3-70B and GPT-4 reasoning help most models; GritLM reasoning helps BM25 but is weaker for others.
limits: Targets StackExchange, coding and theorem questions, not a store of the agent's own solved subproblems. The rewrite is a free-form reasoning trace plus draft answer, not a relation-tag abstraction. Costs one LLM generation per query (length not reported in the text I read).
agent_relevance: Best direct evidence for gap 9: reformulating the probe before search works without training. It is not specific to relational wording; any answer-like expansion may be doing the work.
quote: Searching with LLM reasoning steps significantly improves performance.

source: Su et al. (2025, ICLR) BRIGHT, Table 3 reranking depth
finding: LLM reranking of the top candidates helps a little, and going from top-10 to top-100 does not reliably pay. A cross-encoder trained on web search hurts and gets worse with depth.
numbers: Average nDCG@10, original queries. BM25 alone 14.3; MiniLM cross-encoder top-10 13.1, top-100 8.3; Gemini-1.0 top-10 15.7; GPT-4 top-10 17.4, top-100 17.0. Google embedder alone 19.5; MiniLM top-10 16.0, top-100 9.4; Gemini top-10 20.1; GPT-4 top-10 21.5, top-100 22.6.
limits: Listwise reranking in one prompt, so deeper lists also mean a longer prompt. Single benchmark and two first-stage retrievers. Token cost per setting not given in the text I read.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: a small rerank window (about 10) captures most of the gain; the extra tokens for 100 bought +1.1 for one retriever and -0.4 for the other. Use a top-10 rerank, not a deep one.

source: Sourati et al. (2024) ARN: Analogical Reasoning on Narratives (TACL)
finding: Side-by-side choice does NOT rescue LLMs when surface and structure conflict. Given a query story and two candidates, models choose well when the analogy also looks similar (near analogy vs unrelated distractor) and fail when the structural match is far and the distractor is a near surface match. Humans stay near ceiling in all four cells. So the human pattern 'sound when shown, poor at retrieval' is not the LLM pattern: the LLM failure is already present at recognition.
numbers: Zero-shot accuracy, random 50 percent. (near analogy, far distractor) / (near, near) / (far, far) / (far analogy, near distractor): GPT-4 94.0 / 92.5 / 57.1 / 29.1 (average 68.1); GPT-3.5 88.1 / 81.3 / 50.4 / 21.7 (60.3); SBERT cosine 84.3 / 71.5 / 12.6 / 1.0 (42.3); humans 98.6 / 97.2 / 96.8 / 91.4 (96.0). Average over all models on far analogies 39.6 vs humans 94.1. Models were told to look for system mappings and still failed.
limits: Zero-shot, 2023 models (GPT-4 era), short narratives from proverbs. Far analogies were made semantically distant by SBERT. Newer frontier models not tested; the few-shot results were not read in detail.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 answered for this model generation: a two-way comparison is a weak safeguard against surface decoys. If the agent compares a decoy to a structural match it may still prefer the decoy, so a mapping or verifier step is needed after retrieval.

source: Sultan, Shahaf et al. (2024) ParallelPARC: A Scalable Pipeline for Generating Natural-Language Analogies (NAACL 2024)
finding: With distractors that look like the analogy but reverse the cause-and-effect order, models pick the distractor far more than humans do. Adding such distractors hurts models but not humans. Most of the remaining model errors are choosing the distractor.
numbers: Multiple choice with one analogy, one distractor and random paragraphs: humans 100 percent basic, 96 percent advanced (distractors); GPT-4 95.5 basic, 83.2 advanced. Binary task overall: GPT-4 79.5, Gemini Pro 73.9, ChatGPT 68.2, humans 79 (92.5 after light guidance). Share of mistakes that were the distractor: GPT-4 92.3, Gemini Pro 75.0, ChatGPT 66.9, FlanT5-XXL 62.3, humans 100 (very few errors). Annotator agreement 78.6 percent (chance 25).
limits: Distractors are LLM-generated reorderings of the same paragraph, so they keep surface and break relations, which is the right adversary but not a natural false friend. Small human sample (3 annotators per item). Scientific paragraphs (ProPara).
agent_relevance: Gaps 7 and 6: the best model of that generation lost about 12 points once decoys were added, and nearly all its errors were decoys. A relation-order check (does cause precede effect the same way?) is the kind of cheap test that would catch these.

source: InsightEmb (2026) Learning action-intent embeddings for agentic insight retrieval, arXiv 2608.04761
finding: Inside a multi-step agent loop, re-retrieving a stored insight at every step by plain text-similarity can be worse than no memory at all. A retriever trained to match 'where the agent is in the task' to abstract heuristic rules turned that into a gain. This is a retrieval-key comparison inside the loop, with trajectory-derived insights, at fixed top-1.
numbers: Qwen3-8B agent, top-1 per step, ALFWorld success / WebShop score / ScienceWorld success. No insight 52.86 / 31.03 / 2.40. Base embedder with bundled insights 54.29 / 18.42 / 7.40. Math-trained InsightEmb with bundles 60.71 / 31.74 / 8.00; with single-rule (atomic) insights 59.29 / 32.05 / 10.20 vs Base atomic 55.00 / 28.25 / 7.40. Gains also at k=3,5 and with GPT-5.2 as the action model. Insight corpus built by distilling successful and failed rollouts.
limits: Trained retriever (Qwen3-Embedding-4B fine-tuned on math), not a zero-training structure key. Insights are abstract rules, so it tests abstract-vs-surface matching, not stored subproblems. Token cost not equalised or reported in the text I read. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Closest published answer to gap 1: key choice matters inside a loop, and a progress-blind key can do net harm (WebShop 31.0 to 18.4). It does not test a hand-built relation key or equal tokens, so gap 1 stays partly open.

source: EconSkills (2026) Studying skill transfer and retrieval for web agents on live economic data, arXiv 2609.19523
finding: A matched abstract skill transfers; the same family's raw successful trajectory does not (it caused early termination); the abstract form is the better write-time representation. The paper cannot say abstraction alone is the cause because the prompts also differ in length and format.
numbers: 100 held-out variants, 3 runs each: no skill 123/300 = 41.0 percent (steps 19.83); one matched skill 148/300 = 49.3 percent (+8.3, McNemar p = .0031; 46 failures fixed vs 21 broken; steps 15.67); one matched raw trajectory 21/300 = 7.0 percent. Per pair: matched skill improved 27 of 100, hurt 12.
limits: Web-data agent, 50 hand-parameterised skills; skill author is an LLM from a seed trajectory. Raw-trajectory comparison is confounded (answer removed, long, different format).
agent_relevance: Gap 5, write-time side: converting a solved case to a parameterised procedure (scope, steps, checks, recovery) is worth about +8 points here and a raw case can be strongly negative. No two-case comparison arm, so the specific benefit of comparing two cases is still untested.

source: EconSkills (2026), full-library deployment study (Table 4)
finding: Loose retrieval causes false transfer. When no same-family skill exists, every skill condition does worse than no skill, even when the agent is told it may ignore the hint. Dumping the whole library is far worse than a small retrieved set. Retrieval used only skill names and purposes (a cheap abstract prefilter), not full procedures.
numbers: 360 tasks, one run each. No skill 101/360 = 28.1 percent (direct-match 66/150 = 44.0; no match 35/210 = 16.7). All 50 skills 41/360 = 11.4 percent (18.0 / 6.7; p < 1e-12). Five retrieved 102/360 = 28.3 (48.0 / 14.3; tied with baseline overall, p = 1.0). Five random 88/360 = 24.4 (41.3 / 12.4). One optional hint 93/360 = 25.8 (46.0 / 11.4); on the 210 no-match tasks the approximate top-1 hint cut success 16.7 to 11.4 (p = .043).
limits: One run per task in the library study, so noise is large (differences of 2 points are not significant). Library is only 50 items. 'Direct match' is relative to those 50 families.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: with a forced top-1 and no match, false transfer cost about 5 points, and the polite 'ignore if it does not fit' wording did not remove it. Gap 8: more memory in context can be destructive, so top-k must stay small. Add an explicit no-match option and a mapping check before use.
quote: approximate matches on other tasks offset these gains

source: ThinkRetrieve (2026) Retrieval-augmented test-time scaling inside the reasoning trace, arXiv 2608.10928
finding: Retrieving a solved example at every reasoning step (at the model's own stop-thinking boundary, or a fixed token interval) improves small reasoning models, with token cost counted inside the thinking budget. Gains are largest on the hardest set and for the weakest models; they shrink to about 1 to 2 points on near-saturated sets. This tests mid-loop retrieval of solved problems from a 309,609-item corpus, but with dense embeddings and no structural key.
numbers: Best accuracy over budgets, 3 seeds. AIME 2025 standard thinking / sequential TTS / ThinkRetrieve: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B 14.4 / 23.3 / 30.0; Qwen3-1.7B 24.4 / 22.2 / 35.6; Qwen3.5-2B 17.8 / 31.1 / 34.4; Qwen3-4B 63.3 / 64.4 / 66.7; Qwen3-8B 67.8 / 68.9 / 71.1. GSM8K Qwen3-8B 96.1 / 96.4 / 97.2. Generated tokens 12,913 vs 15,847 at the same budget, about 6 percent wall-clock overhead. Beats self-consistency at equal 8K budget by 16 to 27 points (Qwen3-1.7B, MATH-500 subset). Corpus entries with similarity above 0.90 to a test item removed.
limits: Math only, domain-matched corpus (NuminaMath), sizes 1.5B to 8B. The near-duplicate filter at 0.90 still leaves structural analogs at 0.85 to 0.90 similarity. The authors list as open whether it works when a high-coverage corpus is hard to build. Trigger is the model's own boundary, not a failure signal.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1, 2, 3, 8: shows in-loop retrieval can beat compute-matched alternatives, with a very large memory, and that the benefit falls as the base model gets stronger. Frontier-scale models are not tested.

source: ThinkRetrieve (2026), ablations
finding: Two ingredients matter: retrieval must be inside the trace, and must be relevant. The query that includes the model's current intermediate answer beats a query from the problem alone. Retrieval at the start only gives nothing. Encoder choice barely matters.
numbers: MATH-500, Qwen3-1.7B: query = problem + intermediate answer 91.0 vs problem only 90.2; BERT, E5-Base, E5-Large all 90.87 to 91.27; static input-level RAG 88.80 vs no retrieval 89.07. Table 1: random per-step exemplars sit between sequential TTS and ThinkRetrieve on every cell; static in-context k=3 hovers near the baseline. Help-vs-hurt on Qwen3-4B MATH-500: 26.5 percent of problems helped, 2.0 percent hurt (McNemar p = 5.9e-12 at 12K).
limits: Differences between encoders and query forms are under 1 point and from small subsets. The random-exemplar arm shows part of the gain comes from the injection act itself (a second look with new text) rather than relevance.
agent_relevance: Gaps 2 and 9: a state-aware query (current partial answer) is a cheap form of reformulation, and the best time to retrieve is mid-trace. But 'always on at every boundary' was never compared with 'only when stuck'.

source: Jiang et al. (2023) Active Retrieval Augmented Generation (FLARE), EMNLP 2023
finding: Confidence-triggered retrieval matches or beats retrieving at every sentence while retrieving for fewer steps, and over-retrieval can hurt. This is the closest controlled trigger-vs-always-on comparison I found, but it is for factual long-form QA and not analogue retrieval.
numbers: Triggering retrieval for 40 to 80 percent of sentences usually gave good results across datasets. On 2WikiMultihopQA exact match plateaus once more than 60 percent of steps retrieve; on StrategyQA performance falls once more than 50 percent of steps retrieve. Forward-looking query (next sentence) beats previous-window query (Table 3).
limits: 2023 models, factual QA. Trigger is low token probability, not an impasse or repeated failure. The authors did not report solve rate per token.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: some evidence that gating beats always-on, with no evidence for analogue retrieval. A failure-gated trigger for the agent is still untested.

source: When Deep Research Agents Stagnate (2026) Retrieval-aware agent control (RAAC), arXiv 2608.15191
finding: Detecting stagnation (new documents add little, query coverage is stuck) and then intervening, redirecting or stopping, cut search calls without losing accuracy. This is a failure-triggered intervention, but it redirects search and does not supply an analogue.
numbers: BrowseComp-Plus, seven agents: search calls down by 14 on average, accuracy up to +10 points (+3 on average). WebWeaver recall 64.9 to 67.2, accuracy 47.8 to 51.3, search calls 75.0 to 50.7. Tongyi-DR accuracy 37.9 to 47.9, calls 77.8 to 33.6. GLM-4.7 calls 50.3 to 36.8. Controller and re-thinker use Claude Sonnet 4.5; signals use Qwen3-Embedding-4B. 61.5 percent of query-agent pairs ended in a stop action and 34.6 percent had an intervention only.
limits: Search-agent setting, not problem solving. The controller itself costs LLM calls (overhead reported as modest; I did not check the exact figure). Not compared with always-on analogue injection.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: supports a stagnation signal as a trigger for a change of approach. The trigger can be unsupervised (novelty, coverage), which suits an agent that has no ground truth.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM Agents Are Experiential Learners (AAAI 2024)
finding: Both write-time abstraction (insights from comparing success and failure pairs) and read-time case retrieval help, and which is stronger depends on the domain. Retrieval by task similarity beat both a reasoning-step key and random choice. Adding the model's own reflections into insight extraction hurt. Insight extraction from only the fixed few-shot examples gave no gain over ReAct.
numbers: Insights-only vs retrieval-only success: HotpotQA 36 vs 31 percent, ALFWorld 50 vs 55, WebShop 37 vs 38. Full ExpeL: HotpotQA 39.0 vs ReAct 28.0, ALFWorld 59.0 vs ReAct 40.0. ALFWorld retrieval key: task similarity 59.0, reasoning-step similarity 48.5, random successful trajectories 42.5. HotpotQA insight variants: insights with reflections 28.0, gpt-3.5 insights 32.0, gpt-4 insights 39.0. ALFWorld retrieval-only over 3 retry rounds: 40.3 to 54.4.
limits: Insights come from many pairs and lists of successes together, so the comparison step itself is not isolated (no 'one pair vs two successes' arm). Closed models of 2023. The key comparison is task-similarity vs reasoning-similarity, not structure vs embedding. The ALFWorld ablation table was read from jumbled text; the mapping of 48.5 and 42.5 to the two keys follows the paper's own prose (random drops most).
agent_relevance: Gap 5: closest LLM data on write-time comparison. Pair-based abstraction needs real success and failure experience to work, but there is no token cost and no read-time-sibling arm, so gap 5 stays open.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Agent Workflow Memory, arXiv 2409.07429
finding: Storing abstract workflows (example-specific values replaced by placeholders, common sub-routines pulled out of several trajectories) beats retrieving the most relevant concrete examples. The LM induction step beat a rule-based copy only on one benchmark.
numbers: Mind2Web cross-task vs a retrieve-most-relevant-examples method (Synapse): +5.0 element accuracy and +4.0 step success. Mind2Web LM-based vs rule-based induction: +2.8. WebArena (gpt-4): LM induction 35.5 percent in 5.9 steps vs rule induction 35.6 percent in 6.3 steps (no difference in success). WebArena overall: +12.0 points over the BrowserGym baseline (51.1 percent relative). Workflows come from offline training examples or from the agent's own online successes.
limits: Web navigation; workflows are action sequences, so abstraction is easy to define. The benefit of abstraction is shown by comparison to a different retrieval method, not a matched ablation. Memory is put in context whole; it is not a retrieval test.
agent_relevance: Gaps 4 and 5: abstracting values away at write time is a cheap, effective prefilter-like step (it removes the surface content that embeddings anchor on). Whether abstraction quality is stable across writes was not measured.

source: Yang et al. (2024) Buffer of Thoughts, NeurIPS 2024
finding: Abstracting the problem into its key elements and constraints first (the problem distiller) and then retrieving a stored high-level template by embedding similarity of the template description works training-free. Removing the distiller hurts, more so on harder tasks. The template store grows as problems are solved and later retrieval gets faster.
numbers: GPT-4 Table 1: Game of 24 standard 3.0, CoT 11.0, ToT 74.0, BoT 82.4; Checkmate-in-One standard 36.4, ToT 49.2, BoT 86.4. About 12 percent of the cost of multi-query methods such as tree-of-thought. Retrieval threshold 0.5 to 0.7 on embedding similarity of the distilled problem to template descriptions. Buffer-manager ablation: 4 rounds of 50 questions per task; accuracy rises with rounds with the manager and stays flat without it. Distiller ablation: bigger drops on Game of 24 and Checkmate than on word sorting and MGSM (figure only).
limits: Distiller and meta-buffer ablations are shown in figures I could not read numerically. Only six coarse template categories. Gains over baselines like ToT may mix the template with the single-query format.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 (partial): a training-free restate-as-elements-and-constraints step before lookup is a standard, working component, and its benefit grows with task difficulty. Gap 4: coarse categories plus a similarity threshold already work; tag consistency was not tested.

source: Qin et al. (2025) Relevant or Random: Can LLMs Truly Perform Analogical Reasoning? BBH results
finding: Beyond maths, self-generated relevant exemplars did help a little on five BIG-Bench Hard tasks, unlike GSM8K and MATH where they were worse than none. So the gain is task-dependent, not generally absent. Still tested mainly on GPT-3.5.
numbers: GPT-3.5, 3 seeds, five BBH tasks (temporal sequences, logical deduction five objects, colored objects, formal fallacies, word sorting): relevant exemplars average 63.2, which the paper says is 1.3 points above no exemplars; relevant beat other types on temporal and logical tasks but lost to none on formal fallacies and word sorting. Relevant row: 60.0 / 51.2 / 76.7 / 51.2 / 76.9. Random-biology row average 60.4. GSM8K and MATH: 500 items sampled per seed; 5 and 3 exemplars self-generated.
limits: GPT-3.5 in the main table (GPT-4o-mini in an appendix I did not read); no reasoning-model arm; no fixed-vetted-set comparison on BBH. The no-exemplar row was lost in text extraction, so the 1.3 figure is the paper's own wording.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: the analogical prompting gain is small and task-dependent for a 2023-class model; no evidence for newer models. A reason to cache vetted exemplars, not to generate them every time.

source: DeepSeek-AI (2025) DeepSeek-R1, prompting engineering note
finding: The developers of a frontier reasoning model report that few-shot examples reduce its performance and recommend zero-shot. This is a one-line observation without numbers, but it points the same way as the small gains for strong models in the analogical-prompting work.
numbers: No figures given.
limits: Anecdotal note. About exemplars in the prompt, not about retrieved analogues injected mid-trace (ThinkRetrieve shows those can help small reasoning models).
agent_relevance: Gap 3: for a strong base model, a fixed pre-prompt of exemplars may hurt. Test retrieval on demand against none, and keep it off for easy items.
quote: Few-shot prompting consistently degrades its performance.

source: Asadolahi et al. (2026) Memory Reward Inflation in Self-Improving LLM Agents, arXiv 2608.00017 (abstract page only)
finding: When the agent stores its own episodes with its own score and retrieves them by similarity, wrong episodes get inflated scores and the agent reuses its own confident mistakes. A de-inflation method gave a modest gain.
numbers: BIRD text-to-SQL execution accuracy: LUCID 56.9 percent; Memento-style self-graded 54.0 percent (+2.9); no memory 52.4 percent.
limits: Abstract page only. Preprint. Text-to-SQL.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: memory writes should be gated by an independent check, not by the agent's self-grade, or false transfer will compound.

source: AURA (2026) Utility-guided adaptive reasoning for text retrieval, arXiv 2610.21030 (abstract page only)
finding: Reasoning before retrieval has a cost: extra reasoning steps can add over-generalised abstractions that lower retrieval specificity, so a small estimator stops the reasoning early. It reaches 34.7 average nDCG@10 on BRIGHT with 2.8 reasoning steps and 96 generated tokens per query.
numbers: Latency 4.6 s with full reasoning down to 0.76 s with adaptive stopping.
limits: Abstract page only. Trained model (4B).
agent_relevance: Gap 9: the reformulation step has diminishing and sometimes negative returns; keep it to one short pass.

source: Behnam and Wang (2026) Causal Memory Policy, arXiv 2610.02070 and Feng et al. (2026) EARM, arXiv 2608.22767 (abstract pages only)
finding: Two memory-retrieval preprints point at the same limit: similarity scores alone do not show which memory is useful. CMP says memories that are never retrieved have unknown value, and per-query utility does not predict value on new queries. EARM says LLM relevance scores from past queries can be reused to rerank, giving small gains with a falling scoring bill.
numbers: CMP: identification fails for 54 percent of required memories on LongMemEval and 67 percent on LoCoMo; AUC for separating required from non-required memories 0.54 to 0.66 with random slots. EARM: up to 6.62 percent higher answer accuracy than semantic retrieval; still effective with only 17.5 percent of candidates LLM-scored.
limits: Conversation-memory benchmarks, not problem solving. Abstract pages only; reranking depth and memory size not reported in what I read.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 8: a fraction of the agent's stored cases will never be retrieved, so their value cannot be learned unless some random slots are kept. A reranker with cached scores can cut the rerank bill.

source: Gick and Holyoak (1980), Exp I, IV and V figures as restated in a review found by search (no primary text opened)
finding: Search-result text restating Gick and Holyoak 1980 gives numbers that disagree with each other, so the primary source is still the thing to check. I could not open the primary PDF this session: the University of Michigan repository returned 403, the UCLA lab PDF host did not respond, and ScienceDirect returned 403.
numbers: Restated figures only: hint 100 percent in Exp I; no-hint 20 percent in Exp IV (3 of 15); 35 to 43 percent in Exp V; elsewhere 10 percent with no analogue and 75 percent with a hint.
limits: Secondary, not opened. Use only as 'range 10 to 43 percent without hint depending on experiment'.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 stays open; K01 should keep range wording.
